transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

Now that I’m supposed to be slowing down with my transition to partial retirement, I feel like I’m always on the go and can’t just sit still and relax, even for a short visit or a quiet meal. I expected my life to finally quiet down, but instead, I feel this constant urge to keep moving.
Have you felt this constant urge to keep moving and difficulty sitting still for most of your life, dating back to your childhood, or is this a relatively new change?

It’s actually a lifelong pattern, though it has become much more noticeable over the last eight months since I started cutting back on my teaching hours. Even back in primary school, my teachers always complained to my parents that I couldn't stay in my seat, was constantly chatting, and would constantly get up to wander the room or sharpen my pencils.
Alongside this physical restlessness, do you also struggle with focusing on tasks, organizing your daily activities, or easily getting distracted?

No, I don't really struggle with focusing, organizing, or being easily distracted. As a school teacher, I've actually always been quite organized and able to manage my tasks. My main issue is really just this intense physical restlessness and the constant urge to keep moving.
Do you also find yourself frequently interrupting others during conversations, blurting out answers before a question is finished, or struggling with impatience when waiting your turn?

Yes, I actually struggle with that a lot. I often catch myself jumping into other people's sentences during meetings or finishing my husband's thoughts at home, blurting out my ideas before they are even finished. I only realize afterward that I've cut them off, and it's never my intention to be rude.
At what specific age do you recall these symptoms of restlessness and interrupting others first starting to cause noticeable difficulties for you?

These difficulties go all the way back to my early childhood, definitely well before the age of 12. Even back in primary school, my teachers were constantly telling my parents that I couldn't stay in my seat, was always chatting, and would keep getting up to sharpen my pencil or wander the room. It was a noticeable issue even then, though we didn't really have a name for it back in those days.

This presentation specifically aligns with Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive type (ICD-10 code F90.1), which is now the primary candidate.

This could represent Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1) manifesting as physical tension/restlessness, Adult ADHD (F90.9) with persistent hyperactivity ('driven by a motor'), or a hypomanic episode (F30.0) characterized by increased activity and energy. Further exploration of the nature of this restlessness, its onset, and associated symptoms is needed.

Thus, the candidates are updated to F90.8 and F90.9.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong pattern of hyperactive and impulsive symptoms, including physical restlessness, difficulty sitting still, and a tendency to interrupt others or blurt out answers. These symptoms have been present since early childhood (well before age 12) and have caused persistent functional impairment, particularly noticeable during her transition to partial retirement. She explicitly denies significant symptoms of inattention, which aligns with the predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation of Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ICD-10: F90.1).
